rows.title: A new Colorado hospital opens this weekend. It’s built with the lessons of COVID in mind.
rows.standfirst: Lutheran Medical Center is moving from its longtime home in Wheat Ridge to a new campus near Interstate 70 and West 40th Avenue.

rows.title: “Calm but freaked out”: Estes Park business owners hunker down as fire and tourism seasons collide
rows.standfirst: As the frequency of fires increases during peak tourism season, Estes Park business owners look for ways to help the community

rows.title: What’s Working: As food-insecurity funds end, Colorado farmers focus on food hub, ag incubator
rows.standfirst: East Denver Food Hub, Ag and Food Lab and others got a good start. Now, it’s on to the economic unknown. Plus: Denver 2024 minimum wage will be $18.81, DEN airport reaches new heights, more!

rows.title: Big city water buy-ups in the Lower Arkansas Valley are raising alarms as age-old battles erupt again
rows.standfirst: Aurora, Colorado Springs and Pueblo say they’re trying new methods to better protect farming communities after the water leaves. But bad memories linger in dry, rural areas, and calling it a “lease” may not help.

rows.title: A local developer wants to build on an idyllic meadow. Fraser residents are fighting to protect it.
rows.standfirst: A Grand County trial is set for Aug. 5 as a nearly 20-year battle over conservation at Cozens Meadow erupts in lawsuits, stalled construction and rejected plans for homes.

rows.title: Investors fear a property tax cap could stifle attainable housing development in Colorado
rows.standfirst: Municipal bond investors are threatening to leave Colorado if voters approve Initiative 50, putting the state’s largest source of infrastructure funding for new development in jeopardy

rows.title: Colorado once again breaks tourism records with 31% increase in travelers in the last decade
rows.standfirst: Colorado hosted 93.3 million visitors who spent $28.3 billion in 2023. Spending by tourists supported 188,000 jobs and generated $1.8 billion in state and local tax revenue in 2023.

rows.title: All the new minimum wages in Colorado that kick in Jan. 1
rows.standfirst: Minimum wage goes up every year in Denver, Boulder County, Edgewater and the whole state of Colorado. Here’s why.

rows.title: Colorado resort communities want to impose a vacancy tax on unoccupied homes
rows.standfirst: The legislative agenda for the Colorado Association of Ski Towns includes a first-ever vacancy tax as well as a real estate transfer fee on all property sales to help fund affordable housing

rows.title: Plan to drill 166 wells near Aurora Reservoir OK’d with requirement to use cleaner, quieter electric equipment
rows.standfirst: Lowry Ranch neighbors aren’t ending the fight, saying they will pressure Colorado regulators on safety, noise and wildlife disturbances as the individual drilling sites are considered

rows.title: What’s Working: Market recovers but here’s why Colorado job growth is slowing
rows.standfirst: The number of jobs continues to grow in the state but at a slower rate. There are still some concerns though. Plus: Unemployment claims, local layoffs and more

rows.title: The economics of eating out have some of Denver’s top chefs dismayed, discouraged and looking elsewhere
rows.standfirst: A busy restaurant doesn’t mean thriving. But it’s more than just rising labor and costs and food inflation. Some of the city’s award-winning chefs get specific about their love/hate relationship of being part of Colorado’s largest dining scene.

rows.title: Farms and farmers markets support food-insecure families. Can these initiatives meet growing demands?
rows.standfirst: Programs including coupons that double the value of food assistance spent at Colorado farmers markets are popular, but far fewer people are using them than the state hoped

rows.title: Number of new Colorado businesses drops 21.7% nearly a year after filing-fee discount ends
rows.standfirst: CU Leeds economists saw the sharpest decline in new business filings since 2005. But the other financial trends seem to say business is just getting back to normal.

rows.title: Nearly 10,000 people are homeless in the metro area, but fewer are sleeping on Denver’s streets
rows.standfirst: Homelessness increased by 12% in Denver, though the number of people sleeping outside decreased for only the second time in recent history

rows.title: Denver inflation slowed faster than the national rate to 1.9%. Does it feel like it?
rows.standfirst: Economists say falling housing prices have brought down inflation faster than the U.S. rate of 2.9% in July.

rows.title: Colorado governor calls special session on property taxes to avoid ballot measure fight in November
rows.standfirst: The special session will allow lawmakers to advance a deal under which the conservative supporters of Initiatives 50 and 108 will pull their measures from the ballot

rows.title: Has a Purina pet food plant been in Denver for nearly 100 years?
rows.standfirst: Purina opened a livestock feed plant in Denver in 1930. In 1972, the plant switched to producing pet food.

rows.title: Golden bike maker sues Gates Corp. over unpaid royalties for bike frame invention
rows.standfirst: Spot Brand bikes designed a bike frame for Gates chain-replacing belt and partnered with Gates on a patent. Spot now says it’s owed millions in unpaid royalties.

rows.title: Colorado food banks may soon run out of the federal funds they use to buy local produce
rows.standfirst: Colorado received close to $12 million in pandemic-era funding to help food banks buy local produce, but the money is running low with no replacement in sight

rows.title: What’s Working: This guy wants to get rid of endless phone loops, junk fees and other consumer irritants
rows.standfirst: Rohit Chopra, director of the federal agency to protect consumers, visited Colorado this week. Plus: Loads of state economic news including the July jobs report, unemployment, inflation and more!

rows.title: Are US wind farms killing thousands of birds?
rows.standfirst: Estimates of annual bird deaths linked to wind turbines in the continental U.S. ranged between 230,000 birds and 600,000 birds per year in 2013 and 2014.

rows.title: Steamboat Springs paddleboard pioneer sells Hala, Colorado Kayak Supply after pandemic whiplash
rows.standfirst: Peter Hall started Hala with $30,000 in 2011 and now he’s sold to a longtime employee. He also sold his online paddlesports marketplace to Denver’s Confluence Kayaks

rows.title: Colorado is automatically sealing more than 100,000 criminal records
rows.standfirst: The new law, called the Clean Slate Act, automatically seals misdemeanors after seven years and some felonies after 10 years so they are not visible on background checks

rows.title: Colorado nonprofit aims to help kitchen workers cut stress, embrace healthier habits
rows.standfirst: In The Weeds works to reduce substance abuse and improve mental health among restaurant employees in Four Corners region

rows.title: Eldora Mountain Resort listed for sale as Utah-based operator Powdr sheds ski areas
rows.standfirst: Powdr owner John Cumming is selling Vermont’s Killington and is prepping three other resorts in Colorado, British Columbia and Oregon for sale

rows.title: How the U.S. patent office expanded innovation in Colorado in the past 10 years
rows.standfirst: Being on the ground in Colorado helped the patent office reach inventors where they live — and double its staff in size in five years.

rows.title: What’s Working: Colorado incentives are helping rural firms transition to employee ownership
rows.standfirst: Rocky Mountain Steel in Olathe is the latest to switch to employee ownership, thanks to tax credits and cash for collateral. Plus: Are fewer Coloradans employed than we thought?

rows.title: Colorado’s special session on property taxes may be a bumpy ride
rows.standfirst: It’s increasingly uncertain if the deal Polis struck to cut taxes and prevent a pair of November ballot measures will survive. Many lawmakers aren’t happy about being called back to the Capitol to approve a deal they never agreed to.

rows.title: When are Colorado’s last coal-fired power plants closing?
rows.standfirst: About a third of Colorado’s electricity is still generated by 10 coal-fired power plants. That should drop to zero by the end of 2031.

rows.title: Colorado lawmakers cry foul over draft oil and gas rules revisions reducing, limiting industry oversight
rows.standfirst: Colorado legislators and environmentalists say regulators softened latest proposal after industry pushback

rows.title: A private equity investor turned a Colorado company over to its employees. He’s not the only one.
rows.standfirst: Rocky Mountain Steel in Olathe is the newest Colorado company to go 100% employee owned, with help from the Office of Economic Development and International Trade. New president Dylan Wiman says the model could narrow the wealth gap in Colorado.

rows.title: Colorado lawmakers pass property tax deal that aims to stop November ballot measures
rows.standfirst: The passage of House Bill 1001, which came despite consternation from some liberal Democrats, marks the end of Colorado’s four-day special legislative session

rows.title: Judge dismisses most of Douglas County’s lawsuit against state board that blocked property tax relief plan
rows.standfirst: Denver District Court Judge Martin Egelhoff ruled Wednesday that he lacked jurisdiction to consider the claim brought by Douglas County’s commissioners

rows.title: Colorado short-term rental owners, advocates rally against “heavy-handed regulation” from lawmakers
rows.standfirst: After several years of work to combat state legislation that would increase regulations and taxation on short-term rentals, owners are actively lobbying policymakers

rows.title: What’s Working: How a Colorado program is linking quantum, space and tech companies to a future workforce
rows.standfirst: The state’s externship program has placed teachers at quantum, space and other STEM companies. Will real-life experiences translate into inspiring students?
